verses.translation_literal: A psalm of David. YHWH [is] my shepherd; I will not lack.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song of David, sung low, almost to himself. The LORD is my shepherd. And so there is nothing I will go without.
verses.directors_commentary:
Begin small and certain. Do not play this as a hymn; play it as a man naming the one fact he has stopped arguing with. A shepherd in the ancient Near East was no gentle figure of the nursery: he fed, led, defended and counted the flock, and his work was a standard image for a king, so 'YHWH is my shepherd' is also a claim about who rules the speaker. The speaker is a king, and he is calling someone else the king. The Hebrew superscription 'mizmor' means a song sung to a stringed instrument, and the line has four words only: YHWH, my-shepherd, not, I-lack.

The KJV's 'I shall not want' has aged badly: 'want' meant 'lack', and a modern audience hears 'desire', which flips the sense. The Hebrew is the plain verb 'to be short of', in the imperfect, so it can mean 'I do not lack' as a habit as well as 'I will not lack' as a promise. The Rashi in the packet reads it as spoken in the wilderness, and the Targum has the Lord feeding His people in the wilderness: both fit a speaker on the move.

philological_notes.note: 'My shepherd', literally 'the one who shepherds me': a participle with a suffix used as a noun. In royal ideology of Egypt and Mesopotamia, 'shepherd' is a title for a king, so the image is political as well as pastoral.
'I will lack', 'I am short of'. English 'want' (KJV) meant exactly this; it now means 'desire' and misleads.

verses.translation_literal: In abodes of grass he makes me lie down; beside waters of resting-places he leads me.
verses.translation_dramatic: He settles me down in the green grass, where the herd can rest. He leads me out to the water, and the water is slow and quiet.
verses.directors_commentary:
The camera moves from the shepherd to the flock, and the speaker is now the sheep. Play the verbs: 'makes me lie down' and 'leads me' are things done to him, and he lets them be done. The noon image is exact: in the heat of the day a shepherd stops the flock and lets it lie in shade (Song 1:7, quoted by Radak and Meiri in the packet), and he waters it only at a place where the water does not run fast, because sheep panic in a current and will not drink.

The KJV's 'green pastures' loses the first noun: 'ne'ot' is 'dwellings, encampments' (Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion), the shepherd's own tent site, and 'deshe'' is fresh young grass, which in Judah is green only for a few weeks in the spring. 'Still waters' translates 'mei menuchot', literally 'waters of resting-places': water that is itself at rest and the place where you rest. The commentators read it as slow water as against a rushing wadi (Ibn Ezra, Radak). 'Leadeth' (yenahaleni) is the same verb that Moses sings of God at the Red Sea ('you led in your strength', Exod 15:13, Metzudat Zion in the packet): this shepherd is also a liberator.

philological_notes.note: 'Abodes, encampments', the camp of a shepherd, from nāweh. 'Pastures' in the KJV is the sense by extension; the word is about a home for the flock.
'Resting-places' or 'rests', plural of menuchah. 'Waters of menuchot' is water at rest, or water of a place of rest; Ibn Ezra sets it against a rushing stream.

verses.translation_literal: My soul he brings back; he guides me in tracks of righteousness for the sake of his name.
verses.translation_dramatic: He brings my soul back to me, and I breathe again. He guides me down the straight tracks, the right ones, and he does it for the sake of his own name.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tempo drops again: this is the exhale. 'Nefesh' is not a ghost inside a body; it is the whole living self, throat and breath and appetite, and what is 'brought back' is the speaker's life, as if it had been spent and had run out. Rashi (in the packet) says it is the spirit that had been worn thin by troubles and flight; Radak and Metzudat Zion hear the other sense of the verb, 'he sets it at rest' (as in Isa 30:15, 'in returning and rest you shall be saved').

The KJV's 'paths of righteousness' sounds like a moral lecture. 'Ma'gelei tsedek' is 'tracks', the worn ruts of a cart or a flock's regular route (the word is from the root 'round', 'wheel'): the sheep follows the beaten way and does not stray. 'Tsedek' means 'right', 'what is as it should be', before it means 'virtue'. And then the reason: not 'because I deserve it' but 'for the sake of his name', that is, his reputation as a shepherd is at stake. Radak and Meiri (packet) say it outright: 'not that I am worthy'.

philological_notes.note: Intensive of 'return': 'he brings back' (to its former state, Rashi) or 'he gives rest' (Radak, Metzudat Zion, from Isa 30:15). Both are in play; 'restores' (KJV) covers only the first.
'Tracks, ruts, beaten ways', from the root of 'circle, wheel'. Not abstract 'paths' but the well-worn route.
'For the sake of his name': for his reputation, not for the speaker's merit.

verses.translation_literal: Even [though] I walk in a valley of shadow-of-death, I will not fear evil, for you [are] with me; your rod and your staff, they, they comfort me.
verses.translation_dramatic: And even if my road bends down into the ravine where the dark lies thickest, the valley the old voices call the shadow of death, I will not fear harm. For you are here, at my side. Your rod, your staff: I see them, and they speak peace to me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker turns from "he" to "you" at this verse, and the actor should feel it: after three verses of talking about the shepherd, the sheep now speaks to him, because in the dark he is close enough to address. The pivot is the small word 'imadi, "with me", and the whole verse leans on it. The geography is real: the Judean wilderness is cut by steep, narrow wadis (gey'), where the walls shut out the sun, flash floods arrive without warning, and lions and wolves lie in wait. A shepherd leading a flock between grazing grounds could not avoid these defiles.

The word tzalmavet is the famous crux. The Masoretic vowels give a compound, tzel + mavet, "shadow of death", and that is how the Targum (tula demota) and the KJV take it; Radak and Metzudat Zion read it the same way, as the darkness of the grave, and Radak ties it to Job 10:21. The other reading takes the word as a single noun from tzalam, "deep darkness": this is Dunash ben Labrat, whom Rashi cites ("every tzalmavet is an expression of darkness"), and it is followed by Metzudat David ("a dark valley, that is, a place of danger") and by modern lexicons. Both readings land in the same place for a performer: the valley is darkness and mortal danger together, so the actor can carry both without choosing. The KJV, ASV and Webster's choose "shadow of death"; BBE's "deep shade" and YLT's "death-shade" lean toward the other end.

The last clause stutters on purpose: "your rod and your staff, they, they comfort me", with hemah, "they", resuming the two nouns. The KJV and ASV keep this resumptive "they" (as YLT does), whereas BBE drops it ("your rod and your support are my comfort"). Radak explains the plural verb by the two named things. The shevet is the shepherd's club, for driving off predators and counting sheep; the mish'enet is the staff to lean on and guide with. Rashi and Metzudat David hear in the pair the rod of discipline and the staff of support; Malbim sees the one hand for correcting and the other for warding off wild beasts. Neither tool is a metaphor of luxury: they are simply what a man holds when he walks in the dark.

philological_notes.note: Pointed as tzel + mavet, "shadow of death", and so understood by the Targum and by Radak and Metzudat Zion, for whom it means the darkness of the grave. Others read a single noun, "deep darkness", from tzalam: Dunash ben Labrat via Rashi, Metzudat David, and modern lexicons. The word is used of the grave in Job 10:21-22, and of a murky place elsewhere.

The shepherd's rod or club, a hardwood stick for beating off predators and for counting sheep as they pass under it. The same word also means the rod of discipline and a ruler's sceptre, which is why Rashi and Metzudat David hear affliction in it.
A third-person pronoun placed before the verb, resuming "rod and staff": "they, they comfort me". It adds emphasis, and Radak explains the plural by the two things named.

verses.translation_literal: You arrange before me a table, in front of my adversaries; you have made fat my head with the oil; my cup [is] saturation.
verses.translation_dramatic: You lay a table for me, right there in front of my enemies, and they have to watch. You have poured the oil over my head until it shines. My cup is full, and then fuller than full.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene changes: from the open hillside to a tent, a house, a feast. The speaker is a guest now, and the host is the same protector. The enemies are not defeated, they are not even gone; they are standing at the door and looking in. A meal shared in front of enemies is a public act: in the ancient Near East, to eat at someone's table was to be under his protection and obligated to him, and a host who protected a guest in the face of his pursuers was publicly declaring whose man he was. Radak (packet) says 'that they see my honour and rot with envy'.

The KJV's 'anointest' makes it a present rite, and 'my cup runneth over' reads an overflow into the text. The Hebrew 'dishanta' is a perfect and literally 'you have made fat': oil on the head was a courtesy for a guest at a feast (as the head was sleek and glistening) and also the anointing of a king, which Rashi and Metzudat David in the packet connect to David's own anointing. 'Cup is saturation' (revayah) is a quantity, 'soaked, drenched', and nothing says it spills. Keep the extravagance in the voice, not the spill on the floor.

philological_notes.note: 'You arrange, set in order'; the verb for setting out a table or battle-line. The meal is set out like a battle formation facing the enemy.
'You have made fat', hence 'fresh and sleek' with oil. A perfect, not KJV's present. Rashi and Metzudat David read it as the earlier anointing as king; Radak reads it as a figure for abundance.
'Saturation, drenching', being soaked or full to satisfaction; Rashi says 'a word of satiety', Metzudat Zion compares Ps 65:11 ('its furrows, soak them').

verses.translation_literal: Surely good and covenant loyalty will pursue me all the days of my life, and I will return in the house of YHWH for length of days.
verses.translation_dramatic: Surely, goodness and faithful love will hunt me down, every day of my life. And I will come home, to the house of the LORD, for as long as I have days.
verses.directors_commentary:
End on the door and on the verb. The KJV's 'shall follow me' is the biggest softening in the psalm: the Hebrew is 'yirdefuni', 'they will pursue me', the same verb that is used for the enemies chasing a man in battle. The speaker has been pursued by hostile men (verse 5 'adversaries'); now the pursuers are goodness and covenant loyalty, and they are as relentless as the enemies. Play it as comic relief, if the actor has the nerve: the one who runs away is the speaker, and he is being caught by blessing. 'Chesed' is not 'mercy' but covenant loyalty, the faithful love that a party owes the other in a bond, and the KJV's 'mercy' makes it a forgiveness that is not asked for.

The last line has a famous textual snag. The Masoretic pointing, 'veshavti', is from 'to return': 'and I will return to the house of YHWH'. The Septuagint and Vulgate, followed by the KJV, read it as 'dwell', 'and I will dwell'; Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri (packet) allow both 'come back again and again' and 'be at rest' (as in Isa 30:15). 'For ever' in the KJV also overstates 'le'orekh yamim', 'for length of days', which Radak understands as a long life. The 'house of the LORD' is the sanctuary (Radak: where the ark is). This speaker does not claim eternity; he claims a lifetime of coming home.

philological_notes.note: 'Covenant loyalty, faithful love': the commitment that a person owes in a bond. 'Mercy' (KJV) takes it for a pardon; here it is a gift of faithfulness.
'They will pursue me': the verb of the hunter and the enemy in war. Meiri takes the figure as the good qualities being so close to him that they seem to chase him.
In the Masoretic text 'and I will return' (from shuv), where the KJV has 'dwell' (from yashav). Ibn Ezra and Radak allow 'return again and again' and 'be at rest'.
